I am analyzing some grassland songbird data and am particularly =
interested in the proportion of birds that are estimated to be detected =
at various distances. This is because many other studies simply employ =
fixed-width transects (of many different widths) and assume that all =
birds are observed within the transect.

For example, we usually truncated our data at 100 m because few birds =
were observed beyond that distance. Obtaining an estimate of the =
proportion of birds detected can be obtained from the Distance output. =
However, I would like to know, based on our detection function using all =
observations to 100 m, what proportion of birds were detected at 25, 50 =
and 75 m from the line.

Would truncating the data to 25 m and and forcing the program to use the =
detection function and parameter estimates from the analysis using all =
the data provide a correct estimate of p at 25 m ? I realize the SE and =
CIs would be wrong.

Or is there a way to take the full model and estimate p for distances =
<=3D25 m, and possibly calculate a 95% CI using the var-cov matrix and =
delta method? My detection functions are either hazard rate or =
half-normal with no adjustment terms. =20

Any suggestions would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Duane

> > I am analyzing some grassland songbird data and am particularly interested in the proportion of birds that are estimated to be detected at various distances. This is because many other studies simply employ fixed-width transects (of many different widths) and assume that all birds are observed within the transect.
> >
> > For example, we usually truncated our data at 100 m because few birds were observed beyond that distance. Obtaining an estimate of the proportion of birds detected can be obtained from the Distance output. However, I would like to know, based on our detection function using all observations to 100 m, what proportion of birds were detected at 25, 50 and 75 m from the line.
> >
> > Would truncating the data to 25 m and and forcing the program to use the detection function and parameter estimates from the analysis using all the data provide a correct estimate of p at 25 m ? I realize the SE and CIs would be wrong.
> >
> > Or is there a way to take the full model and estimate p for distances <=25 m, and possibly calculate a 95% CI using the var-cov matrix and delta method? My detection functions are either hazard rate or half-normal with no adjustment terms.

Duane, you will find amongst the output in Distance the following:

Model
Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*A(1)**2))


Point Standard Percent Coef. 95 Percent
Parameter Estimate Error of Variation ConfidenceInterval
--------- ----------- ----------- -------------- --------------------
A( 1) 8.391 1.420 16.93
f(0) 0.14416 0.65386E-02 4.54 0.13187 0.15758
--------- ----------- ----------- -------------- --------------------

For the hazard-rate, it will look slightly different. With no
adjustments, just substitute A(1)=8.391 (in this particular data set) into
k(y), and evaluate at the required distances.

To get ci's, you could select the bootstrap option in Distance, and
calculate the probabilities as above for each resample, using output from
the bootstraps. This requires some programming external to Distance, and
you will need to check the Distance help files to see how to access output
from the resamples.

Steve Buckland
